analysis.one_liner: Conditions federally backed financing for manufactured home parks on basic tenant protections like 60-day notice of rent increases.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2021 with 5 House supporters but never received a committee vote or floor action before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Millions of Americans live in manufactured home communities where they own the home but rent the land under it, leaving them exposed to sudden rent increases or eviction from the park. This bill said that owners of those communities could not get federally backed loans - through HUD mortgage insurance or purchases by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac - unless they gave residents baseline protections: one-year renewable leases, 60-day written notice of rent increases (with even longer notice for larger hikes), a five-day rent grace period, the right to sell their home in place, and 60-day notice before a park is sold or closed. It also created penalties - paid to tenants - for owners who violated these terms, and set up a commission to propose stronger protections.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of manufactured home communities, who are disproportionately low-income, older, and rural. Roughly one in ten rural households lives in a manufactured home, and because they rent the pad under their home, an owner's rent hike or park sale can leave them unable to afford to move the home out. The bill would give residents advance notice of increases, protection from arbitrary eviction, and cash penalties when owners violated their rights [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Manufactured home residents who rent their lot

how_it_helps.text: Requires one-year renewable leases with good cause required for non-renewal, and 60-day written notice of rent increases - with 30 extra days of notice for every additional 2.5% increase above 5% - so residents can plan or negotiate instead of facing sudden hikes [S3].

Gives tenants a five-day grace period on rent, a right to cure defaults, the right to sell their home without moving it out of the park (including within 45+ days after eviction), the right to post a For Sale sign, and written reasons for any termination or denial [S3].

Creates real money penalties paid to injured tenants - for example, 6 months of rent for wrongful termination, and repayment of any improper rent increase with interest plus 25% - and bars violating owners from federally backed financing for at least 3 years [S3].

Makes the protections a condition of federal money: HUD could not insure, and Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac could not purchase, loans for building, rehabilitating, or buying manufactured home communities unless the borrower certifies the protections for every community it owns, and requires a public website listing covered properties [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners of manufactured home communities - including large corporate and institutional investors that have been buying up parks - would face limits on how fast they can raise rent, new notice obligations, tenant-enforced penalties, and the risk of losing access to federally backed loans if they do not comply [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Park owners and corporate community investors

drawbacks.text: The protections only bind owners who seek federally backed financing; owners who rely on private lenders could continue current practices, so many communities would remain uncovered [S3].

Lenders and the government-sponsored enterprises argued-for loan channel could shrink: making loans harder to qualify could reduce financing for new park construction and rehabilitation, which in theory limits the supply of affordable lots [S3].

Compliance and enforcement would add administrative burden for small park owners, and the tenant-paid penalties (such as 20% of a community's sale price split among residents for a sale-notice violation) could be difficult to calculate and litigate in practice [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents, the bill offered genuine protections against practices that can strand families in homes they cannot afford to move. The main cost falls on owners' flexibility to raise rents, and the financing condition could modestly reduce the flow of capital into the sector. The bill was deliberately narrow - tied to federal loan programs and explicitly preserving stronger state laws [S3] - so its costs are limited, but so is its reach: it would have protected only communities whose owners touch federal financing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never received a markup, committee vote, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Cynthia Axne introduced the bill on May 19, 2021, with Rep. Ro Khanna as an original cosponsor [S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, the only committee action ever recorded [S5] [S1].
Four House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor appeared [S4].
No further action - no subcommittee or full-committee markup, no report, no floor vote - was ever taken through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023, and the bill died there [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of manufactured home communities, including corporate park investors, are better off: they keep unrestricted freedom to raise lot rents and sell or close parks without the notice requirements and tenant penalties the bill would have imposed. The tenants who would have gained protections got nothing, and federal loan programs continue to finance communities without any attached tenant rights.

for.name: Rep. Cynthia Axne
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Manufactured Housing Tenant's Bill of Rights Act of 2021 in the House [S3].

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's original cosponsor at introduction [S3].

against.name: Chair Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a subcommittee or full-committee markup, leaving it without any committee action or path to the floor for the rest of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no split is on the record; all five supporters in the record were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored [S4].

industries.industry: Manufactured home community owners and investors
industries.note: Park owners - including the large corporate buyers that have consolidated the sector - would have lost the ability to raise lot rents quickly, evict without cause, or sell and close parks on short notice, and would owe tenants cash penalties for violations. Their interest in unrestricted rent increases runs directly against residents' need for stability [S3].

industries.industry: Lenders and loan investors serving manufactured home communities
industries.note: HUD, Fannie Mae, and Freddie Mac could no longer back loans for communities that lack the tenant protections, which could shrink lending volume to the sector but also make the federal loan channel dependent on owners accepting resident protections. Compliance documentation would add costs for lenders [S2] [S3].
